words.definition: Cheerfully optimistic and confident about how things will turn out.
words.example: Despite the losing streak, the coach stayed sanguine about the team's chances.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'sanguis' (blood); old medicine tied a blood-rich temperament to rosy red cheeks and a cheerful outlook.

words.definition: Feeling or showing anger at something seen as unjust or offensive.
words.example: She grew indignant when the waiter blamed her for his own mistake.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'in-dignity' — an attack on your dignity fills you with angry protest.

words.definition: Serious and thoughtful, or not under the influence of alcohol.
words.example: After the accident, he took a sober look at his reckless driving habits.
words.mnemonic: Read it as an acronym: S.O.B.E.R. — Serious, Observant, Balanced, Even, Reasonable.

words.definition: To give a formal statement of evidence, especially in a court of law.
words.example: The witness agreed to testify about what she saw the night of the robbery.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'testis' (witness); on the stand your account is put to the 'test'.

words.definition: A doubt about something, or an arrangement made in advance to secure a place.
words.example: I have my reservations about the plan, but I'll go along with it for now.
words.mnemonic: Think 're-serve' — you hold something back: a seat kept aside, or your full agreement held back by doubt.

words.definition: To describe or tell the details of an event or experience.
words.example: Over dinner, grandfather would recount his adventures at sea.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-count' — you go back over each item one by one, telling every detail of the story.

words.definition: A detailed written record of events arranged in the order they occurred.
words.example: Her diary became a chronicle of life during the war.
words.mnemonic: 'Chrono' means time (Greek 'chronos'); it lays out events by the clock and calendar.

words.definition: To show or represent something in a picture, words, or performance.
words.example: The mural depicts farmers working in the fields at harvest time.
words.mnemonic: It hides the word 'pict' — as in picture; to depict is to paint a picture of it.

words.definition: To describe or represent someone or something in art, writing, or acting.
words.example: The novel portrays the king as a lonely, frightened man.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'portrait' inside it — an actor or painter presents a subject as a portrait.

words.definition: To communicate a message or feeling, or to carry something from one place to another.
words.example: Her trembling voice conveyed just how frightened she really was.
words.mnemonic: Think 'conveyor belt' — it carries objects along; you carry meaning across to a listener.

words.definition: To compare two things in order to show how they differ.
words.example: The essay contrasts city life with the quiet of the countryside.
words.mnemonic: 'Contra' means against; you set two things against each other to spotlight their differences.

words.definition: To mention or hint at something indirectly rather than saying it openly.
words.example: During the speech she alluded to the scandal without ever naming anyone.
words.mnemonic: 'A-LUDE' sounds like 'a low-key clue' — you drop a subtle hint instead of stating it.

words.definition: The right to vote in political elections.
words.example: Women in the United States won suffrage in 1920.
words.mnemonic: 'Suffer-age' — activists suffered for ages before earning the ballot.

words.definition: The right to vote, or an authorization to run a business using a company's brand.
words.example: The new law extended the franchise to citizens over eighteen.
words.mnemonic: From Old French 'franc' (free) — being granted the freedom to vote or to trade under a name.

words.definition: A direct public vote on a single political question.
words.example: The country held a referendum on whether to join the European Union.
words.mnemonic: Starts with 'refer' — the government refers one question straight back to the people.

words.definition: A direct vote in which an entire population decides a specific political question.
words.example: The government called a plebiscite to let citizens themselves decide whether to join the union.
words.mnemonic: 'pleb' (the common people) + 'cite' (to summon) — the common people are summoned to vote.

words.definition: An official elected assembly with the power to make and change a nation's laws.
words.example: The bill finally passed the legislature after months of debate among the elected representatives.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'legis' (of law) + 'lature' (a structure) — the structure built for making law.

words.definition: To formally pass a proposal and put it into effect as law.
words.example: Congress voted to enact stricter safety rules after the factory disaster.
words.mnemonic: 'en-' (to make) + 'act' — to turn an act into binding force.

words.definition: To formally reject or forbid a decision made by a lawmaking body.
words.example: The president chose to veto the bill, blocking it from ever becoming law.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'veto' literally means 'I forbid' — the word a Roman tribune shouted to stop a measure.

words.definition: To rule and control the affairs of a country, region, or organization.
words.example: The council was elected to govern the city for the next four years.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'gubernare', to steer a ship — a leader steers the ship of state.

words.definition: To act as an official authority who formally settles a dispute or decides a case.
words.example: A neutral panel was appointed to adjudicate the bitter contract dispute between the two firms.
words.mnemonic: 'ad-' (to) + Latin 'judic' (judgment) — to bring judgment to a quarrel.

words.definition: To assign a task or authority to another person to act on your behalf.
words.example: A good manager will delegate routine work so she can focus on strategy.
words.mnemonic: 'de-' + Latin 'legare' (to send) — to send someone in your place to do the job.

words.definition: The person who currently holds a particular political office or position.
words.example: The incumbent lost the election to a younger challenger promising sweeping change.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'in-come-bent' — the one already IN, comfortably bent into the seat.

words.definition: A local official who administers the law and hears minor legal cases.
words.example: The magistrate fined the reckless driver and dismissed the more serious charge.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'magister' (master) — a master of the local law.

words.definition: Complete honesty and strong moral integrity in one's conduct.
words.example: The auditor's reputation for probity made everyone trust her final report without question.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'probe' and 'prove' (Latin 'probus', good) — a person proven good.

words.definition: Morally correct behavior and firm adherence to what is right.
words.example: His unwavering rectitude meant he refused every bribe without a moment's hesitation.
words.mnemonic: 'rect' means straight (rectangle, correct) — moral straightness that never bends.

words.definition: Fairness and impartiality in the way people are treated.
words.example: The new policy promotes equity by giving every student equal access to laptops and tutoring.
words.mnemonic: 'equi-' means equal (equator, equilateral) — treating everyone on equal, fair terms.

words.definition: A state in which citizens elect representatives and there is no monarch.
words.example: After the king was deposed, the nation became a republic led by an elected president.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'res publica' means 'the public thing' — the state belongs to the public, not a crown.

words.definition: The dominant influence or control of one nation or group over others.
words.example: For decades the empire's naval hegemony went unchallenged across the entire region.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'hegemon' (leader); say 'he-JEM-ony' — the leader who holds all the gems of power.

words.definition: To seize a territory and incorporate it into an existing state.
words.example: The empire moved to annex the neighboring province, redrawing the border overnight.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'an-next' — grabbing the next patch of land over and bolting it on.

words.definition: To formally leave a larger group, nation, or alliance to become independent.
words.example: Several southern states chose to secede from the Union before the war began.
words.mnemonic: Root: se- (apart) + cedere (to go) = to go apart. Picture a region quietly walking out the exit door of a nation.

words.definition: A formal written request signed by many people asking an authority to act.
words.example: Residents signed a petition demanding the city repair the crumbling bridge.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'pet' — imagine pestering an official with a pet request, clipboard in hand, until they finally listen.

words.definition: To try to influence lawmakers or officials in favor of a particular cause.
words.example: Environmental groups lobbied Congress to pass stricter emissions limits.
words.mnemonic: Picture activists crowding the marble lobby of the capitol, buttonholing politicians as they pass through.

words.definition: To go through an area seeking votes, opinions, or support from people.
words.example: Volunteers canvassed the neighborhood, knocking on every door to discuss the candidate.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'canvas' — imagine stretching one huge canvas over the whole district so you cover every single house.

words.definition: Speech or action that stirs people to rebel against the governing authority.
words.example: The pamphlets urging soldiers to abandon their posts were condemned as sedition.
words.mnemonic: Root: sed- (apart) + itio (a going) — whipping up a crowd to go apart from the state.

words.definition: The crime of betraying one's own country, especially by aiding its enemies.
words.example: Passing military secrets to the enemy during wartime is punishable as treason.
words.mnemonic: From Latin tradere, 'to hand over' — a traitor hands the whole nation over to its foes.

words.definition: An open rebellion by sailors or soldiers against their commanding officers.
words.example: The crew staged a mutiny, seizing the ship from its tyrannical captain.
words.mnemonic: Think 'Mutiny on the Bounty' — the famous shipboard revolt where the crew throws the captain overboard.

words.definition: To openly resist or refuse to obey an authority, rule, or expectation.
words.example: She defied her parents' curfew and stayed out well past midnight.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'de-FIE!' — shaking a fist and shouting defiance right in authority's face.

words.definition: To openly disregard a rule, law, or convention with contempt.
words.example: Drivers who flout the speed limit endanger everyone on the road.
words.mnemonic: Don't confuse with 'flaunt.' Picture tossing the rulebook 'out' the window — fl-OUT, out it goes.

words.definition: To act against or violate a law, rule, or established principle.
words.example: Building the shed without a permit contravened the local zoning code.
words.mnemonic: Root: contra- (against) + venire (to come) — to come up against the rule and cross it.

words.definition: To break a moral or legal boundary by overstepping accepted limits.
words.example: He transgressed the terms of his parole by leaving the state.
words.mnemonic: Root: trans- (across) + gradi (to step) — to step right across the line you were told not to cross.

words.definition: To act in accordance with a request, command, or set of rules.
words.example: All restaurants must comply with health and safety regulations.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'come + ply' — you come along and bend (ply) yourself to the rules.

words.definition: To accept or agree to something reluctantly but without protest.
words.example: Though she disliked the plan, she acquiesced rather than argue any further.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'quiesce' (quiet) — you go quiet and let it happen, silently giving in.

words.definition: To stop resisting and surrender, usually on agreed terms.
words.example: After months under siege, the exhausted garrison finally capitulated.
words.mnemonic: From capitulum, the 'headings' of surrender terms — picture a white flag raised over the capital as both sides sign the chapters.

words.definition: Loud, harsh, and grating in sound, or insistently forceful in tone.
words.example: Her strident voice cut straight through the noise of the crowded hall.
words.mnemonic: 'Stride + dent' — a harsh voice that comes striding in and dents your ears.

words.definition: Presenting a strongly biased view meant to promote a particular cause.
words.example: The documentary was so tendentious that it ignored every fact contradicting its thesis.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'tend' + 'tenacious' — it stubbornly tends toward one side.

words.definition: Feeling or showing deep and solemn respect.
words.example: The pilgrims fell silent, reverent, as they stepped into the ancient shrine.
words.mnemonic: Think 'revere' and 'reverend' — a reverend treats the sacred with awe.

words.definition: The condition of being lawful, rightful, or widely accepted as valid.
words.example: Observers questioned the election's legitimacy after thousands of ballots went missing.
words.mnemonic: Root 'legit' from Latin lex/legis — something in line with the law.

words.definition: Obligated to explain or take responsibility for one's actions.
words.example: Voters demanded that officials be held accountable for how the money was spent.
words.mnemonic: You must give an account — count up — of everything you did.

words.definition: The act of supervising or watching over a process or group.
words.example: A congressional committee provided oversight to ensure the agency obeyed the rules.
words.mnemonic: Over + sight — someone watching over things from above.

words.definition: All the citizens who are entitled to cast votes.
words.example: The candidate toured rural towns hoping to win over a skeptical electorate.
words.mnemonic: 'Elector' + '-ate' — the collective body of those who choose leaders.

words.definition: Not supporting or controlled by any political party.
words.example: A nonpartisan commission redrew the districts without favoring either side.
words.mnemonic: 'Non' negates 'partisan' — not taking any party's part.

words.definition: Involving agreement or cooperation between two political parties.
words.example: The bill passed with rare bipartisan support from both sides of the aisle.
words.mnemonic: Bi = two; a compromise where two parties join forces.

words.definition: Reliable, commanding, and accepted as accurate or true.
words.example: She gave an authoritative account of the case, citing every relevant statute.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'author' — the author of the definitive text speaks with weight.

words.definition: Showing that you regard something as unworthy of serious attention.
words.example: He gave a dismissive wave, refusing even to hear the proposal.
words.mnemonic: To 'dismiss' is to send away — you wave ideas away.

words.definition: Showing moderation and self-restraint, or having a mild climate.
words.example: Even when provoked, she stayed temperate and never raised her voice.
words.mnemonic: Keep your 'temper' controlled — hold it in check.

words.definition: An official count of a population, often recording details about people.
words.example: Every ten years the census asks how many people live in each home.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'sense us' — the government tries to sense us all by counting.

words.definition: A paper or process used to cast a secret vote in an election.
words.example: She marked her ballot carefully and slipped it into the sealed box.
words.mnemonic: From Italian 'ballotta,' a little ball once dropped in a box to vote.

words.definition: The skill of managing relations between nations, or handling matters with tact.
words.example: Through patient diplomacy, the envoy averted a war between the rival states.
words.mnemonic: Think 'diploma' — a diplomat is credentialed in smoothing over conflicts.

words.definition: The theory, philosophy, or study of law and legal systems.
words.example: Her thesis in jurisprudence explored why unjust rules still command obedience.
words.mnemonic: 'Juris' (law) + 'prudence' (wisdom) — the wisdom behind the law.

words.definition: The period during which someone holds a position, office, or property.
words.example: During her tenure as mayor, three new libraries opened across the city.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'ten years' — picture a professor guaranteed her job for ten-ure, a long secured stretch of holding a post.

words.definition: An official agreement or state of harmony between people or groups.
words.example: After months of tense talks, the two nations signed an accord ending the border dispute.
words.mnemonic: Think 'a chord' — separate notes struck together in harmony, just as parties come into agreement.
